title: Merging step: from a 4-term solution to a 3-term one (when do two unit fractions sum to a unit fraction?)
connection: 1/a + 1/b = 1/c iff (a − c)(b − c) = c². Given many 4-term solutions of 4/n, ES follows if some pair satisfies this. The density of 'mergeable pairs' among 4-term solutions is a computable statistic.
why: Reduces ES to a statement about 4-term solutions (easier to construct) plus a quadratic coincidence; a 4-term family with a built-in mergeable pair would be a Type I/II family in disguise.
first_step: For n ≤ 2000 enumerate 4-term solutions with bounded denominators and count mergeable pairs; check whether every n has one (it must, since ES holds there).

title: Octonions / Cayley integers: non-associative ES — category check
connection: Unit fractions in a non-associative algebra are still defined (x⁻¹ = x̄/N(x)), and sums make sense, integer scalars still associate, so n·x scaling arguments survive; what may fail are arguments multiplying non-real denominators together (products of three octonions). The world is meaningful but its structure theory is thin.
why: Low value except as a test of which ES arguments use associativity (probably none beyond commutative subalgebras).
first_step: Low priority; note.

title: Numerator 4 over F_q[T] with A = T² + 1 irreducible of degree 2 (an 'odd 4')
connection: F_q[T] with q odd has |A| = q² for degree-2 A. Choosing A irreducible makes the numerator 'prime', unlike 4 = 2². Comparing A = T² and A = T² + 1 (q = 3) tests whether a reducible numerator matters (batch A item) — this is the companion run.
why: If irreducible A has more exceptions, the reducibility 4 = 2·2 helps over Z (e.g. via 2-adic structure).
first_step: Run the existing FF search for q = 3, A ∈ {T², T² + 1, T² + T + 2} for deg P ≤ 10.
areas: ES variants, function fields & other rings

title: Odd greedy algorithm as a cautionary every-n problem
connection: The odd greedy expansion (always choose the smallest odd denominator) is conjectured to terminate for every rational with odd denominator, but this is open even though Breusch/Stewart show odd representations exist. ES has the same split: existence vs a specific algorithm. Keep proofs about existence, not about a fixed procedure (consistent with B1's bounded-procedure barrier).
why: Prevents investing in 'prove algorithm X always succeeds' routes that are harder than existence.
first_step: Run the odd greedy algorithm symbolically on 4/n and determine the exact condition under which it terminates within three terms.
alt_first_steps: [upgrades-0299] List ES approaches in the repo that are algorithmic (fixed search order) and mark which could be restated as pure existence.
[free_opus-0007] Check current status of odd greedy termination (Guy UPINT D11) and whether any partial result used a monovariant that has an ES analogue.
[signature-0079] Compute min k such that 4/p − 1/(⌈p/4⌉+k) is a sum of 2 unit fractions, for hard primes ≤ 10⁹; study the distribution of k.
refs: R. K. Guy, Unsolved Problems in Number Theory, D11

title: Feature: parameter family crossing the dividing line
connection: Dividing-line feature 'parameter family crossing the dividing line'. ES IS the endpoint m = 4 of Schinzel's m/n family (Pomerance–Weingartner transition at p ≈ exp(m^{1/2+o(1)})). To supply it one could: prove a monotonicity/interpolation statement: solvability of m/p for m' < m at all large p; or uniform-in-m count lower bounds
why: Families that cross (5x+1 vs 3x+1, Hensley δ, m/n) localise where proof techniques stop.
first_step: Compute R_m(p) for m = 4..20 and the same p; check whether R_m(p)·m/(log p)³ is stable (PW heuristic) and whether m = 4 shows anomalous excess.

title: Feature: monotone structure in the number of terms k
connection: Dividing-line feature 'monotone structure in the number of terms k'. ES ES is k = 3; k = 2 completely classified (Stewart); k ≥ 4 has power counts. To supply it one could: use the k = 2 classification as a sieve: ES(p) holds if some explicit p-tied integer N has a coprime-divisor pair (a,b) with 4 | a+b … i.e. reduce to many k = 2 problems
why: Interpolating between a classified and an open case is a classic route.
first_step: Formalise: ES(p) ⟺ ∃x: 4/p − 1/x is a 2-term fraction; apply Stewart's criterion to (4x − p)/(px) for x in [p/4, 3p/4].

title: Between: Schinzel's N_m growth exponent
connection: Pomerance–Weingartner predict N'_m = exp(m^{1/2+o(1)}); proving any upper bound N_m < ∞ for one m ≥ 4 would be ES-strength.
why: Locates ES (m = 4) on a curve; if exceptions at m = 8..15 follow the Poisson model precisely, the model's prediction 'no exceptions for m = 4' is calibrated.
first_step: Fit observed largest exceptions (PW table: m=8: 241; m=12: 12241; m=15: 20521) against exp(c·m^{1/2}) and against (log p)³/m ≈ const.

title: Between: Why is m = 12 so exceptional in the Pomerance–Weingartner table?
connection: m = 12 has 24 exceptions up to 10^12 vs 9 for m = 10 and 13 for m = 13; the count per m should correlate with an arithmetic singular series (structure of (ℤ/m)^× and −1).
why: An 'ES singular series' S(m, n) that predicts the m-dependence would be the right object to bound below at m = 4.
first_step: Compute heuristic expected counts E_m(p) = Σ_{Type I/II shapes} densities for m = 4..15 and correlate with exception counts.

title: Between: Ternary Egyptian for numerators m with all denominators in an AP
connection: 4/n = 1/x + 1/y + 1/z with x,y,z ≡ r mod q: local obstructions appear; which (q,r) still look universal?
why: Maps local obstructions vs global failures in a controlled family.
first_step: Compute for q ≤ 12 the residues r for which all n ≤ 10^6 coprime to stuff are solvable.

title: Between: Erdős's log log b terms conjecture
connection: Every a/b with ≪ log log b terms; Vose gives √log b.
why: Uniform bounded-term phenomena for general a; ES is a = 4 with 3 terms.
first_step: Read Vose 1985 and Tenenbaum–Yokota; check whether their methods give O(1) terms for 4/p on a density-one set (known anyway) or something new.

title: Catalog: Pomerance–Weingartner j-unit-fraction generalisation
connection: Pomerance–Weingartner j-unit-fraction generalisation ↔ ES as a small-count existence problem. Expected witnesses/n: ≈ (log p)^{2j−3}/m-type (check). Obstruction: none. Status: proved generalisation of the exception bound to j terms (per abstract). Mechanism: Elsholtz–Tao-style counting.
why: Two-parameter (m, j) family; ES at (4, 3).
first_step: Read the j-term section of arXiv:2511.16817 and extract the predicted transition curve in (m, j).

title: Minimal pair: m/n, m large, p ≈ exp(m^{1/3}) (mostly false) vs m = 4 (ES, open, verified 10^18)
connection: m/n, m large, p ≈ exp(m^{1/3}) (mostly false) vs m = 4 (ES, open, verified 10^18): they differ essentially in one feature — expected count (log p)³/m crossing 1. ES's position: ES sits far on the large-count side for every p ≥ 2; the transition is a pure count transition with no arithmetic obstruction.
why: Minimal pairs isolate the feature responsible for crossing the dividing line; each is a precise question about ES.
first_step: See PW calibration items.

title: Minimal pair: k = 2 Egyptian (classified by Stewart) vs k = 3 Egyptian (ES, open)
connection: k = 2 Egyptian (classified by Stewart) vs k = 3 Egyptian (ES, open): they differ essentially in one feature — one more unit fraction: from a single divisor-class condition to a union over a 2-parameter family. ES's position: The k = 2 criterion is the gate; ES is a union of k = 2 gates.
why: Minimal pairs isolate the feature responsible for crossing the dividing line; each is a precise question about ES.
first_step: See 'k=2 reduction' feature item.

title: ES as a 'prime covering' dual to Sierpiński: an explicit infinite system that must cover all primes
connection: Sierpiński numbers are k such that a finite covering hits every k·2^n + 1; ES is the claim that an infinite AP system {−f mod 4ad} hits every prime. Both are covering statements, one about a sequence, one about primes.
why: Unifies the failure mechanism of p + 2^k with the success claim of ES: covering theory is the common language.
first_step: Survey: are there theorems that an infinite family of APs with divergent Σ1/modulus and a 'genericity' condition covers all primes (or all integers) except an explicit set?

title: Erdős–Graham problem on 4/n with distinct denominators all ≤ n^{1+ε}?
connection: Bounding the largest denominator changes count; there might be literature on 'Egyptian fractions with small denominators' (Erdős–Graham book) for 4/n specifically.
why: A family where the count is tunable by the size bound.
first_step: Check Erdős–Graham 'Old and new problems' section on unit fractions for size-bounded ES variants.

title: Ramsey–ES: a monochromatic solution for every finite colouring (stronger statement)
connection: Croot proved every finite colouring has a monochromatic Egyptian representation of 1. Formulate Ramsey–ES: for every finite colouring of ℕ and every large prime p, is there a monochromatic (x,y,z) with 4/p = 1/x + 1/y + 1/z? If true, it implies ES and may be accessible to Croot-type density arguments (or be false, which is informative).
why: Strengthenings sometimes have better proofs; falsification would show which colourings are 'ES-hard'.
first_step: Test colourings by 2-adic valuation parity, by residue mod 3, and random 2-colourings for p ≤ 10⁴; look for primes with no monochromatic solution.
refs: arXiv:math/0311421 (Croot, On a coloring conjecture about unit fractions, Ann. Math. 157 (2003))
areas: ES variants, function fields & other rings

title: Failure sets are monotone under divisibility of the numerator (sanity + structure)
connection: If m | m′ then fail(m) ⊆ fail(m′) (multiply all denominators of an m′/n representation by m′/m to get one of m/n); verified on all m ≤ 48, p ≤ 10⁵. 'Primitive' failures (not explained by a divisor d ≥ 5 of m) number 0,0,1,6,4,8,3,22,10,8,25,32,17,45,…
why: ES is the bottom of a divisibility lattice of Schinzel problems; primitive failure counts strip out inherited obstructions and are the right 'new difficulty' per numerator.
first_step: Submit primitive-failure counts to OEIS; examine whether primitive failures of 4k concentrate on primes hard for 4/p.
refs: arXiv:2511.16817 (Pomerance–Weingartner, Exceptions to the Erdős–Straus–Schinzel conjecture)

title: Hardness index H(p) = #{m ≤ 48 : m/p fails} correlates with U(p)/log²p (ρ = −0.43)
why: A single prime-level 'obstruction profile' across numerators: if hardness were a local (Euler-product) phenomenon, H(p) should be predictable from p mod small numbers — a cheap test of locality.
first_step: Regress H(p) on Legendre symbols (q/p) for q ≤ 30 and on p mod 8,9,16,25; report R².

title: PW numerics reproduced: for every m ∈ [20,48] some prime in (m², 2m²) fails m/p
connection: Counts of failing primes in (m², 2m²): m=20:6, 21:5, 22:5, 23:5, 24:13, …, 48:70 — consistent with PW's reported numerics for m ≥ 20.
why: Independent confirmation of a 2025 literature claim with our engine; and the counts per m give an empirical density to compare with PW's probabilistic model.
first_step: Compare the counts with PW's predicted number (their Elsholtz–Tao-style density) in (m², 2m²).
refs: arXiv:2511.16817 (Pomerance–Weingartner, Exceptions to the Erdős–Straus–Schinzel conjecture)

title: 10/n fails at {2,3,7,11,43,61,67,181}; 11/n at {2,3,4,37}; 13/n at {2,3,4,5,7,14,53,61,67,79,211,281}
connection: Complete-looking small exception lists (n ≤ 4000 all, primes ≤ 10⁵), none in OEIS; composite exceptions occur (4 for 11 and 13, 14 for 13).
why: Each list is a finite certificate target; the presence of composite exceptions (4, 14) shows the reduction-to-primes fails for m ≠ 4, unlike ES.
first_step: Explain 13/14 and 11/4 failures (why multiplicativity breaks) and check whether any composite n > 100 fails m/n for m ≤ 13.

title: 15/p failure set contains three of the 30 hardest ES primes (4201, 12601, 20521)
connection: 15/p fails at 25 primes ≤ 10⁵ ending 1103,1171,1367,4201,6301,12601,16831,20521; 4201, 12601, 20521 are top-30 hard for 4/p though 15 is not a multiple of 4.
why: Cross-numerator coincidence not explained by divisibility monotonicity; suggests a shared local cause (p ≡ 1 mod 120 or 840?).
first_step: Compute p mod 840 for 15/p failures and test enrichment of p ≡ 1 (mod 120).

title: Number of m/p failures ≤ 10⁵ by m: 0,0,1,6,4,8,3,22,10,9,25,38,17,49,16,63,… (no OEIS match)
connection: The failure-count profile across m (5..48) has strong arithmetic modulation (peaks at m ≡ 0 mod 12).
why: A Fourier/arith analysis of this profile would expose which local factors (mod 3, mod 4) drive Schinzel failures.
first_step: Regress log(#fail(m)+1) on log m and the indicator functions 4|m, 3|m, 5|m.

title: 12/25 fails while 12/5 fails: inherited, but 13/14 fails with 13/2, 13/7 failing
connection: Composite failures appear to be products of failing primes (25 = 5², 14 = 2·7, 4 = 2²): consistent with 'fail(m/n) ⇒ each prime factor fails or is tiny'.
why: If 'n fails ⇒ every prime factor of n fails' held for all m it would reduce Schinzel to primes as for ES.
first_step: Test the implication on m ≤ 48 and n ≤ 4000 composite (needs composite runs for m > 13).

title: Schinzel sibling with j unit fractions (PW's generalisation)
connection: PW also treat m/n as a sum of j unit fractions; the analogous fingerprints (failure sets of m/n with j=2,3,4) give a two-parameter table.
why: The j=2 case is purely divisor-theoretic (m/n = 1/x+1/y ⟺ divisors of n² in a class) — an exactly solvable layer whose failure statistics calibrate j=3.
first_step: Note 4/n = 1/x + 1/y is solvable iff n is even or has a prime factor ≡ 3 (mod 4), so its exceptional set (all prime factors ≡ 1 mod 4) has density zero — the same set as the isosceles-law failures; compute and the j=4 exceptions for m ≤ 48.
refs: arXiv:2511.16817 (Pomerance–Weingartner, Exceptions to the Erdős–Straus–Schinzel conjecture)

title: Primes failing ≥ 15 numerators are all < 700
connection: High H(p) occurs only at small p (113, 193, 101, 137, 181, 421, 149, 241, 281, 353, 397, …); for p > 10⁴, H(p) is small.
why: Shows that 'multi-numerator hardness' decays with p — consistent with Vaughan-type almost-all results with explicit m-dependence (PW).
first_step: Plot max H(p) over dyadic ranges.

title: Candidate explanation of the q mod 3 dichotomy: p ≡ −3 (mod q) forces (p/q) = (−3/q)
connection: The strongest single shift is x = (p+3)/4 (ρ(U, τ(p+3)) = +0.48); q | p+3 ⟺ p ≡ −3 (q), which forces (q/p) = (p/q) = (−3/q) = +1 iff q ≡ 1 (mod 3). So for q ≡ 1 (3) 'q is a QR' is positively confounded with 'q divides p+3' (more solutions), cancelling the generic negative QR effect.
why: Candidate mechanism (not yet tested by the controlled regression in the first step): the greedy first step x = ⌈(p+1)/4⌉ couples ES counts to the cubic-residue-flavoured symbol (−3/q). Every first-denominator shift s similarly couples via (−s/q).
first_step: Verify by adding 1[q | p+3] features; then search for the full 'shift ⊗ character' structure: weight of (q/p) ≈ Σ_s w_s·(−s/q)·(…).

title: Reversal: does the count law predict which numbers m/p fail (Schinzel)?
connection: Use the fitted ES-count Euler product with numerator-m analogue to predict log U_m(p); compare predicted lowest values with actual failures m ∈ [8, 48].
why: A successful prediction would show the Schinzel failures are exactly 'local-density-small' primes — supporting PW's probabilistic picture with arithmetic content.
first_step: Fit per-q weights for each m (data on disk) and compute AUC of predicted log U_m for failure vs non-failure.

title: ES hardness vs 'p − 1 practical number' (Erdős–Graham denominators)
connection: p − 1 practical (every m ≤ p − 1 a sum of distinct divisors) is common for smooth p − 1; hard primes have smooth p − 1; Egyptian-fraction representability of 1/p-type fractions is classically tied to practical numbers.
why: Links ES hardness to the practical-number literature (Vose, Saias), where Egyptian fraction lengths are controlled by divisor richness.
first_step: Compute 1[p − 1 practical] and its correlation with residual U(p); check whether all 30 hardest primes have p − 1 practical.

title: ES solution denominators and the Prouhet–Tarry–Escott / Znám problem: category check
connection: Znám's problem (each n_i divides ∏_{j≠i} n_j + 1) and Egyptian-fraction 'improper' problems share unit-fraction identities; ES solutions with x | yz + 1-type divisibilities could be fingerprinted.
why: Low expectation; recorded as a breadth item because Znám-type divisibility is the 'Sylvester sequence' world where unit-fraction identities are exact.
first_step: Count ES solutions at primes with x | yz ± 1 or y | xz ± 1 and see if any family is universal.

title: Sierpiński 5/p hard primes: 8821, 6301, 4201, 12601, 81901, 4621, … all ≡ 1 (mod 20)
connection: Hardest primes for 5/p (residual log U₅) ≤ 10⁵; 4201, 12601, 20521 are also among the hardest for 4/p; residual correlation between U₄ and U₅ is only +0.23.
why: Primes ≡ 1 modulo a smooth number are hard for every numerator (shared 'p − 1 smooth' axis) while the character axes differ by numerator — a decomposition of hardness into universal and numerator-specific parts.
first_step: Fit the Euler-product law for 5/p (per-prime weights) and compare its signs with 4/p.

title: Cross-numerator residual correlations: U₄ vs U₅ 0.23, U₆ 0.50, U₇ 0.16, U₉ 0.26, U₁₃ 0.15
connection: Residual log counts at primes 10³–10⁵ correlate weakly across numerators except 6 (6/p = (4/p)·(3/2) shares structure with 4/p).
why: Different numerators see largely different arithmetic: a joint 'all numerators hard' prime must be p ≡ 1 mod a smooth modulus — 12601 = 2³3²5²7 + 1 is hardest for 4, 5 and 7 simultaneously.
first_step: Cluster primes by their vector of residuals over m = 4..13; identify the universal-hard cluster.

title: 12601 = 12600 + 1: hardest prime across numerators 4, 5, 7
connection: 12601 has U = 27 (rank 26 of 8 966 primes ≡ 1 (4) ≤ 2·10⁵ by U/log³p), is rank 4 for 5/p and rank 1 for 7/p, and fails 15/p; p − 1 = 2³·3²·5²·7.
why: A natural single test case for 'universal' hardness, smaller than 2521-type examples for other numerators.
first_step: List all ES solutions of 4/12601, 5/12601, 7/12601 and identify common structure (denominators' factorisations).

title: U(p) vs U((p+3)/4): raw Spearman 0.66; vs U(4p+1): 0.36 (size-confounded)
connection: Raw rank correlations between ES counts at p and at the p-tied integers (p+3)/4 and 4p+1 (p ≤ 30 000 / 7 500).
why: Most of this is the common size trend; the residual correlation (after log n terms on both sides) would show whether difficulty propagates along the greedy map p ↦ (p+3)/4.
first_step: Recompute on residuals; if positive, ES-hardness is 'inherited' along the greedy forest (FOREST_*.md).

title: Fraction splitting trees
connection: Connect ES identities to the elementary split 1/a=1/(a+1)+1/(a(a+1)), allowing merges as well as splits.
why: Length-three targets might be reached through longer identities with controlled cancellation or merging.
first_step: Generate a bounded graph of positive unit-fraction identities connected by exact splits and inverse merges.

title: Combinatorial games on residual fractions
connection: Define legal moves as exact split-and-merge operations and winning positions as positive three-term decompositions.
why: A strategy theorem on a specified class of positions could produce constructive identities.
first_step: Write precise game rules, enumerate small positions, and look for a decreasing potential on winning strategies.

title: Bloom-related density increments
connection: Investigate whether work associated with Bloom on unit-fraction problems offers a density-increment mechanism adaptable to structured divisor sets.
why: The potentially transferable object is a lemma about reciprocal mass, not an assumed three-term theorem.
first_step: Find the relevant paper, verify its hypotheses, and compare its denominator set with divisors of a p-tied integer.

title: Odd-denominator greedy variants
connection: Compare a greedy rule restricted to odd denominators with unrestricted greedy search on related residual fractions.
why: Restrictions can expose parity mechanisms even if they make termination harder.
first_step: Define a precise odd-denominator choice rule and compute its first three residuals on a bounded set of admissible rational inputs.

title: Two-term and four-term boundary cases
connection: Compare the rigid two-term equation and more flexible four-term constructions with the three-term target.
why: A controlled bridge might identify the exact extra degree of freedom that must be eliminated.
first_step: Start from an explicit four-term identity and solve the exact condition under which two terms merge to one.

title: Characteristic sensitivity of the numerator
connection: Separate characteristics dividing four from those where four is invertible before importing finite-field analogies.
why: In characteristic two the numerator vanishes, so an unqualified transfer would be mathematically misleading.
first_step: Compare the cleared equation in characteristics 2,3,5 and explicitly label degenerate components.
areas: ES variants, function fields & other rings

title: Reciprocal additive energy modulo q
connection: Study additive relations among inverses of a structured denominator set in a finite field.
why: This is a direct modular analogue of the reciprocal sum and can identify concentration or additive structure.
first_step: Choose an odd prime q not dividing p; compute the additive energy of inverses of a short nonzero interval in Fq and compare its three-fold sums with 4/p modulo q.

title: Dyson's 'sphere-packing of unit fractions' metaphor: energy minimization over Egyptian fraction triples
connection: Treat (x,y,z) as particles with energy E = |4/n − 1/x − 1/y − 1/z|; ES is 'ground state energy is 0 for every n'. Energy-landscape methods (basin-hopping, simulated annealing) find ground states fast; the landscape's funnel structure might reveal a deterministic descent rule.
why: A deterministic descent that never gets stuck would be a proof; even failing that, the funnel geometry around the global minimum may suggest an invariant.
first_step: Run basin-hopping on E over (x,y,z) ∈ [1, n²]³ for 1000 primes; record the sequence of local minima visited and check whether they correspond to continued-fraction convergents of 4/n.

title: Gravitational lensing time-delay identities and unit fractions
connection: Fermat's principle for multiple images gives sums of reciprocals of distances; integer-distance lensing configurations are an unexplored source of Egyptian fraction identities (pure lead-check).
why: Cheap search; probably nothing.
first_step: Web search 'reciprocal distances integer identities lens equation Egyptian'; drop if nothing.

title: Knuth–Bendix / term rewriting view of the 'Egyptian fraction identities' and confluence
connection: The family of identities (e.g. 1/n = 1/(n+1) + 1/(n(n+1))) forms a rewriting system on multisets of unit fractions; ES asks whether 4/n rewrites to a 3-element multiset. Confluence/termination theory could classify reachable lengths.
why: Formal rewriting makes 'what can be derived from splitting identities' a decidable question in restricted cases; the known tiny families (Bleicher–Erdős) would fit.
first_step: Define rewriting rules: split 1/a → 1/(a+1) + 1/(a(a+1)), merge 1/a + 1/b → 1/c when possible; compute reachable 3-term representations from the greedy 4-term one for n ≤ 1000.

title: Lattice attack on 'ES with x fixed to the greedy choice': when does greedy-first-term lead to a two-term remainder?
connection: The Fibonacci–Sylvester greedy picks x = ⌈n/4⌉; the remainder (4x−n)/(nx) with 4x − n ∈ {1,2,3} is a two-term sum iff a divisor condition on nx holds. For 4x − n = 1: 1/(nx) is one unit fraction, so greedy gives 2 terms? No: n ≡ 3 mod 4 case gives 1/(nx) — that's the easy class. For n ≡ 1 mod 4, 4x − n = 3 and 3/(nx) must split into two unit fractions.
why: The hard class p ≡ 1 mod 4 is exactly 'is 3/(p·⌈p/4⌉) a sum of two unit fractions, or else choose a non-greedy x'; the two-term criterion for 3/m is classical (3/m = 1/a + 1/b iff m has a divisor pattern mod 3). Making the 'non-greedy x' choice explicit is the whole game and the lattice view (x free, divisor of p²x² in class) is clean.
first_step: Tabulate for p ≤ 10⁶ the smallest x ≥ ⌈p/4⌉ such that (4x−p)/(px) is a two-term Egyptian fraction; study x − ⌈p/4⌉ distribution (is it O(log p)? polylog?).

title: Rational curves of higher degree on U_n/ℚ(n) with floor/sqrt: 'Puiseux identities'
connection: Mordell–Schinzel kills polynomial identities (rational curves over ℚ(n)) on square classes. But identities over ℚ(√n) (i.e. n = m² and x,y,z polynomials in m) are allowed and exist (the m² case has solutions from m). The question for primes: identities over ℚ(n^{1/k}) are not applicable since p is not a k-th power — but identities over ℚ(√(n+a)) could apply when n+a is a square. A 'union over a' cover? Each a covers a sparse set (n = m² − a), total density 0 — so no, unless a varies with n. Record and drop? Keep as an item: 'Schinzel's theorem for algebraic-function identities'.
why: Clarifies what algebraic-function identities can and cannot do; Schinzel may have covered it.
first_step: Search 'Schinzel identities Erdős–Straus algebraic function of n'; read Schinzel 2000 'On sums of three unit fractions with polynomial denominators'.
alt_first_steps: [upgrades-0276] Search polynomial X, Y, Z of degree ≤ 4 in m for k = 1, 2, 3, 5, 7 (with congruence conditions on m), via undetermined coefficients.
refs: arXiv:2005.02998 (Skorobogatov-Sofos, Schinzel Hypothesis on average and rational points)

title: Analogy: Erdős's 'every n > 1 is a sum of distinct unit fractions with denominators ≤ …' — the greedy/Bleicher–Erdős bounds on the number of terms vs denominators; the 3-term boundary
connection: The theory of representing rationals as sums of k unit fractions with denominators ≤ D (Bleicher–Erdős 'Denominators of Egyptian fractions') gives tradeoffs between k and D; ES is k = 3, D unconstrained; maybe a tradeoff theorem 'k = 3 with D ≤ n² always' is provable with the same tools in a weakened form (e.g., k = 3 for all n outside a set of size ≪ N/(log N)^A — the Vaughan line).
why: Historical method check.
first_step: Read Bleicher–Erdős 1976 'Denominators of Egyptian fractions' II and see the structure of their k-term bounds for a/n.

title: Information from the literature on 'n + u has a divisor in a residue class mod u-dependent modulus' — search specifically for 'divisors of consecutive integers in prescribed classes' and 'Erdős problem on d | n + k with d ≡ ... mod k'
connection: The shifted reparametrisation suggests searching the Erdős problem corpus (erdosproblems.com has ~1000 problems) for anything about divisors of n + k in classes depending on k.
why: Erdős posed many 'consecutive integers' divisor problems; one may be ES-equivalent or ES-adjacent with known partial results.
first_step: Full-text search erdosproblems.com for 'divisor' + 'consecutive' / 'n+k'; read the hits.

title: Bloom–(shifted primes) unit fractions as a test of 'prescribed-denominator-shape' methods
connection: Bloom's 'Unit fractions with shifted prime denominators' (arXiv:2305.02689) represents 1 with denominators p−1 ↔ ES denominators are constrained to be multiples of p or p-tied.
why: A method that works with arithmetically constrained denominators is closer to ES's constraint than free-denominator results.
first_step: Read 2305.02689 abstract/intro and list which constraint (shifted primes) survived the Fourier argument and why; ask if 'denominators ≡ 0 mod p' is analogous.

title: Sierpiński 5/n and Schinzel m/n as a family: uniform-in-m translation
connection: The m/n = 1/x+1/y+1/z conjectures (Schinzel: for n ≥ n₀(m)) share U_n's geometry with 4 replaced by m. T1-type obstructions should exist at m-dependent square classes.
why: A translation that works for all m simultaneously (e.g. a fibration over m) might reveal which part of ES is specific to 4.

title: Four unit fractions are easy: why 4/p = four terms is trivial and what the 4→3 step loses
connection: 4/p = 1/x1+…+1/x4 always solvable (e.g. via greedy) ↔ ES 3 terms; the 4-term solution set is a 'thick object' and ES asks it to degenerate.
why: A collapse map from 4-term to 3-term solutions (merging two fractions with sum a unit fraction) is an extraction rule in the G1 sense.
first_step: Count 4-term solutions with two terms summing to a unit fraction; check whether that count is ≍ the 3-term count or larger (identity check).

title: The unit-fraction 'Erdős–Graham r/s with denominators in a set' (Erdős #, Bleicher) problem
connection: Which rationals have representations using denominators from a prescribed set ↔ ES: denominators from the p-tied set.

title: The 'Egyptian fractions with prime denominators' problem (Erdős–Graham) and ES with prime z
connection: Sums of reciprocals of primes equal to 1/n or rationals ↔ ES solutions where denominators are constrained.

areas: ES variants, function fields & other rings

title: Rav, Schinzel–Sierpiński polynomial identities (no identity for square classes) as a Galois-theoretic obstruction
connection: Mordell–Schinzel: no polynomial identity solves ES on a residue class containing squares ↔ Galois/monodromy of the solution variety over ℚ(n).
why: The obstruction is 'no rational section'; asking for multi-sections of bounded degree or sections over ℚ(√n) or ℚ(n^{1/k}) is a natural relaxation.
first_step: Search for algebraic (non-polynomial) identities: solutions x(n),y(n),z(n) ∈ ℚ(√n) or ℚ(√(n+c)) that specialise to integers for many n.

title: Erdős–Graham 'bound on the number of solutions' (Browning–Elsholtz upper bounds) as a structural pressure
connection: Browning–Elsholtz bounded the number of solutions of m/n Egyptian 3-term equations from above ↔ lower bound needed.
why: Upper-bound techniques (divisor bounds on a determinantal parametrisation) give the parametrisation used for lower bounds too.
first_step: Read Browning–Elsholtz 'The number of representations of rationals as a sum of unit fractions' (Illinois J. Math. 2011?) and extract its parametrisation.

title: Moree/Pomerance–Weingartner on m/n exceptions as numerator-uniform calibration
connection: Pomerance–Weingartner study the m/n three-unit-fraction exceptions ↔ ES m=4; their density heuristic for exceptions as m grows.
why: Their exception-generation mechanism (n in specific residue classes making all slices fail) is exactly what ES must avoid; reading why it can't occur for m=4 is a structural lemma target.
first_step: Extract PW's mechanism for exceptions at m=8 (n=131, 241) and test whether a 'virtual' m=4 version exists at some modulus.

title: Dirichlet series of ES solution counts and multiple-zeta-like structure
connection: Multiple zeta values have Egyptian-fraction-flavoured sum structure ↔ generating functions of ES solution counts.
why: Generating function Σ_n f(n) n^{-s} for ES counts may be expressible via double/triple Dirichlet series with MZV-like structure.
first_step: Check whether a paper on Dirichlet series Σ f(n)n^{-s} of Egyptian counts exists (search 'Dirichlet series number of Egyptian fraction representations').

title: Bunyakovsky/Schinzel H ⟹ infinitely many ES-hard-for-small-menu primes (sanity: unconditional disproof shapes)
connection: Under Schinzel H, for any finite menu of certificate types there are infinitely many p evading it ↔ B1 barrier.
why: This is known (B1). Including as calibration of any proposed proof: it must use an unbounded menu.
first_step: Already in repo (B1); first step: check that every item in this list proposes an unbounded menu or flags otherwise.

title: Brownian / random-walk model for the greedy remainder chain
connection: Successive remainders in Egyptian expansions as a Markov chain ↔ probability the chain hits numerator 1 at step 2.
why: Gives a heuristic per-p probability that simple algorithms succeed; separates algorithmic from existential difficulty.
first_step: Simulate the 'first-term then remainder' chain over all first terms x ∈ [p/4, 3p/4] and record the success probability distribution per p.

title: Meta: switch target to ES with 4 replaced by a variable numerator in a family where m = 4 is the boundary
connection: Uniformity in m (E_m results) ↔ find a family statement S(m) true for m ≤ 7 and false for m = 8 whose proof might be easier because it 'knows' the threshold.
why: Threshold-aware statements (e.g. depending on m mod something or size of m) might be provable via local data at m.
first_step: Tabulate small-numerator exception sets (m = 5..12, n ≤ 10⁶) and look for a statement distinguishing m ≤ 7 from m = 8 (e.g. local solubility of an auxiliary variety).

title: Origami / Fujimoto approximation of 1/n folds and Egyptian fractions
connection: Origami folding of fractions (binary folding sequences) ↔ unit-fraction decompositions.
why: Curiosity-level; binary folding corresponds to dyadic expansions, unlikely helpful.
first_step: Skip unless outreach; first step: check if 'folding 4/p in three folds' has a natural formulation.

title: Category-theoretic: ES as existence of a morphism in a category of 'Egyptian decompositions'
connection: Operads/categories of fraction splittings ↔ composition of decompositions.
why: Probably vacuous, but an operadic view might show ES is about generators of an operad being 'enough'.
first_step: Define operad O(k) = k-term decompositions; check whether 3-term decompositions of 4/p arise as composites of 2-term of other fractions (they do: 4/p = 1/x + (4x−p)/(px)).

title: Four-term rescue size: minimal largest denominator when a 4th unit fraction is allowed to be huge
connection: 4/p = 1/x + 1/y + 1/z + 1/w with w forced large ↔ measures 'ES defect' at p.
why: Gives a continuous difficulty measure even when 3-term solutions are plentiful; correlations with R(p) test whether difficulty is one-dimensional.
first_step: For p ≤ 10⁵ compute the minimal max(x,y,z) such that the remainder 4/p − Σ is a unit fraction 1/w with w ≤ p³; compare with R(p).

title: ES ⇒ m/n is a sum of m − 1 unit fractions for every m ≥ 4 (and 'm−1 terms' is a ladder)
connection: m/n = (m−4)·(1/n) + 4/n, so ES gives m − 1 terms (with repeats). Flip: m/n in m − 2 terms is Sierpiński's 5/n problem for m = 5 (3 terms); for general m it trivially fails at small n (e.g. n = 1), and whether it holds for all large n is to be checked (for fixed 3 terms, Schinzel exceptions grow like exp(m^{1/3+o(1)}), Pomerance–Weingartner). F11, F12.
why: Places ES as the first rung of a ladder 'm/n in k(m) terms'; the threshold function k(m) is a natural object whose known values constrain methods.
first_step: Tabulate, for m ≤ 12 and n ≤ 10⁴, the least k with m/n a sum of k unit fractions; record the first m where k = m − 2 fails.

title: Vose: every m/n is a sum of O(√log n) unit fractions — bounded vs. unbounded term counts
connection: Vose's theorem gives a uniform term bound growing with n; ES fixes 3 terms (F12). Erdős conjectured O(log log n) suffices.
why: Methods that achieve O(√log n) (smooth-number denominators) might give 3 terms for numerator 4 if the smoothness budget is tuned to p.
first_step: Re-read Vose's construction and compute the number of terms it produces for 4/p, p hard, p ≤ 10⁹.
refs: unverified: Vose 1985, Egyptian fractions (Bull. London Math. Soc.)

title: Numerator flip 4 → 8: failures at 17, 131, 241 as an anti-overreach test suite
connection: 8/n has genuine exceptions (11, 17, 131, 241 among primes > 3; recomputed by brute force for p < 400) while satisfying the same local/BM features (needs check). Any ES argument must visibly use a property false for 8.
why: Cheapest filter for candidate proofs: run them on 8/131 and 8/241.
first_step: For each tool collected in this lane, write one line: 'does the argument distinguish 4 from 8?'.

title: Schinzel–Sierpiński: every positive rational is (p+1)/(q+1)? — follows from Hypothesis H; ES's B1 uses H in the opposite direction
connection: Under Schinzel's H many ∀∃ prime statements hold; for ES, H implies every bounded procedure fails (B1 Thm C). Shares F35, F01.
why: Interesting duality: H supplies primes where we want them (for existence) and where we don't (to defeat finite procedures).
first_step: Ask whether H also implies ES (it supplies primes in polynomial families — could it supply divisors in classes?) — likely not, but record why.

title: Shift two unit fractions while preserving exactness
connection: The Egyptian-fraction rewriting operator in arXiv:2003.13229 and ES F12/F14/F27: exact reciprocal decompositions admit local transformations while positivity/parity constrain the result.
why: A local rewrite may move a representation into the denominator congruence classes required by ES without changing the sum.
first_step: Read the operator identity and apply it to a two-term portion of a known three-term ES identity; check whether it preserves three terms and positivity.

title: Parity control in Egyptian-fraction rewrites
connection: Arxiv:2003.13229 explicitly discusses parity in Egyptian fractions, matching ES F12/F27/F29 and the denominator parity constraints underlying ES.

title: Egyptian-fraction rewriting and S₃ normalization
connection: The rewrite identity of arXiv:2003.13229 matches ES F12/F14/F27: local transformations can interact with the S₃ symmetry of the three denominator variables and the positivity boundary.

title: Problem 300: Croot and Liu–Sawhney density bounds
connection: Problem 300 ↔ ES F04, F05, F12, F21, F33: count of reciprocal-sum representations, density bounds, and pointwise-versus-average tension.

title: Problem 301: extremal distinct unit fractions
connection: Problem 301 ↔ ES F04, F12, F14, F27: reciprocal equations with distinct variables, symmetric witnesses, and positivity.
why: This extremal problem studies when a set avoids a unit-fraction equation; its disjoint-set argument could expose structural constraints on ES denominator choices.

connection: Problem 302 ↔ ES F01, F05, F12, F33: density-to-existence, finite reciprocal sums and additive structure.

title: Problem 306: multiplicative prime-factor Egyptian decompositions

connection: Problem 308 ↔ ES F01, F04, F12, F21: existence threshold, reciprocal subset sums and pointwise representation.

connection: Problem 311 ↔ ES F04, F12, F21, F32: a least positive reciprocal sum, controlled denominators and explicit certificates.

title: Problem 314: Lim–Steinerberger reciprocal-sum exponent
connection: Problem 314 ↔ ES F04, F12, F21, F24: extremal reciprocal sum, representation scale and heuristic exponent.
why: Lim–Steinerberger show that consecutive harmonic sums Σ_{n≤k≤m}1/k can exceed 1 by as little as ≪ n^{-2}(log n)^{-5/4+δ} for infinitely many n. This calibrates how closely structured reciprocal sums can approach a target, which bears on ES's fixed three-term constraint.

title: Problem 316: divisor-set partition counterexample
connection: Problem 316 ↔ ES F03, F10, F12, F33: divisor structure, partition obstructions and reciprocal sums.

connection: Problem 319 ↔ ES F04, F05, F12, F21: controlled reciprocal sums, density and discrepancy.

connection: Problem 327 ↔ ES F03, F12, F27, F33: reciprocal-equation equivalence, parity and additive structure.

connection: Problem 313 ↔ ES F03, F06, F12, F29: prime denominators, local conditions and fixed reciprocal identity.

connection: Problem 315 ↔ ES F12, F17, F32: reciprocal expansion, bounded construction steps and certificate length.

connection: Problem 300 ↔ ES F05, F12, F21, F25: abundance theorem versus explicit exceptional cases and pointwise demand.

connection: Problem 301 ↔ ES F10, F12, F15, F33: disjoint reciprocal blocks, fixed-variable divisor fibers and additive-multiplicative structure.

connection: Problem 312 ↔ ES F01, F04, F12, F34: large supply forces a reciprocal sum, multiple candidate families cover targets.

title: Problem 319: reciprocal-set construction and residue-class balance
connection: Problem 319 ↔ ES F03, F05, F12, F20: reciprocal sets, density, congruence balance and character-like averaging.

title: Problem 355: lacunary reciprocal sequence covers an interval
connection: Problem 355 ↔ ES F01, F12, F27, F32: reciprocal expansions, positivity and constructive coverage.

title: Problem 308: subset-sum threshold as a two-term completion probe
connection: Problem 308 ↔ ES F01, F12, F15, F32: universal tail coverage, reciprocal sums and fixed-variable hyperbola completion.

title: Egyptian fraction term-count threshold as a feature flip
connection: MO 212865 asks whether a/n (a > 4) is a sum of k < a unit fractions, e.g. 5/n with four terms; comments note this is open in general (citing Elsholtz, Trans. AMS 353 (2001)) while k ≥ a terms is easy by greedy. Matches F11/F12 and flips the term-count threshold relative to the numerator.
why: Understanding exactly why adding one term trivializes a family may identify which ES reductions must preserve the three-term constraint.
first_step: Read MO 212865 and the Elsholtz (2001) paper it cites; compare the easy k ≥ a regime with the k < a regime for a/n and isolate the algebraic step that fails when one term is removed.

title: More-than-three unit fractions and numerator-dependent exceptions
connection: The MO question asks about k/n as a sum of a fixed number of unit fractions when k>4. This shares F01w/F11/F12/F25 and flips the exact numerator 4: fixed-term existence may become easier or harder with k.
why: A controlled numerator comparison can test whether ES's hard residue classes arise from a special small numerator or persist across nearby numerators.
first_step: On primes p in a small interval, compare the number of three-term representations of k/p for k=3,4,5 and tag each missing k against p's residue classes.

title: Counting distinct unit-fraction solutions, not just proving existence
connection: MathOverflow 229514 asks for the number of strictly increasing tuples with reciprocal sum 1 and reports the unique 3-term solution 1/2+1/3+1/6. This shares F04/F12/F14/F21: an exact representation-count problem with symmetry removed and pointwise counts rather than existence alone.
why: A canonical count framework can clarify what ES's R(p) should count (ordered, unordered, or distinct denominators) and how symmetries affect estimates.
first_step: Adopt the increasing-denominator convention from the MO question and recompute small-prime ES representation counts, comparing them to ordered counts after dividing by S3 orbit sizes.

title: Group class equations naturally generate reciprocal sums
connection: MO 229514 notes that a finite group with n conjugacy classes gives a reciprocal sum equal to 1 using centralizer orders. This shares F01/F12/F14/F33: a structured family of unit-fraction representations arises from a symmetry object and its orbit stabilizers.
why: Although centralizer denominators are usually repeated, the orbit-stabilizer construction offers a structural source of identities and a possible way to build ES certificates from group actions.
first_step: Check whether any finite-group class equation can be normalized to 4/p with three distinct centralizer orders; start with small groups and inspect the resulting divisibility constraints.

title: Frobenius finite exceptions and parameter stratification
connection: Three-generated numerical semigroups share F11,F25,F32: parameter regimes can have exceptional cases and finite certificates. ES has numerator-dependent failures of related Egyptian-fraction statements and explicit finite counterexample lists.
why: Parameter stratification may help distinguish ES exceptional primes by the size or gcd pattern of a witness parameter.
first_step: The ref (Moreno-Frías–Rosales 2025) concerns numerical semigroups with a given Frobenius number and fixed gaps; check whether its parameter stratification (or that in Robles-Pérez–Rosales, dimension three) offers an exceptional-parameter template for ES square classes.

title: Odd greedy algorithm feature flip: unbounded term count
connection: Greedy Egyptian expansion shares ES’s positive unit fractions, universal input, and integer certificates (F01,F12,F27), but typically permits a variable number of terms rather than fixed three. This flip pinpoints bounded-term termination as ES’s core difficulty.
why: The algorithm may yield a baseline decomposition from which terms can be compressed or paired into a three-term representation.
first_step: Compare the first three greedy terms for 4/p against a complete ES certificate and identify a local compression identity.

title: Egyptian fraction identities as local witness transformations
connection: Egyptian fraction problems share F12,F14,F16w,F27: positive reciprocal equations have permutation symmetry and algebraic transformations between representations. ES has the same three-term symmetric witness geometry.
why: Classical splitting identities may transform a failed two-term or constrained witness into a valid three-term one while preserving denominator congruences.
first_step: Enumerate unit-fraction splitting identities preserving denominator divisibility by p and check if they close a missing ES square class.

title: Egyptian fraction counts and sieve moments
connection: ES shares F04, F12, F21, F22 with counting representations by unit fractions. The transferable object is a count of divisor parametrisations rather than mere existence.
why: A lower-tail estimate for representation counts could turn average abundance into pointwise existence.
first_step: Read Elsholtz–Tao, identify their count parametrisation, and test whether the second-moment argument localizes to prime n.

title: General fixed-numerator Egyptian fraction conjectures
connection: Schinzel-type equations m/n as bounded sums share F01, F02w, F11, F12, F25. The contrast between numerator 4 and neighboring numerators is structurally relevant.
why: A proof technique that exploits a special numerator could clarify exactly which arithmetic of 4 matters.
first_step: Compare the known m=4 and m>4 constructions and isolate the first point where constants cease to be uniform.

title: Additive energy of {1/x} and three-fold sums: Bourgain-type sum-product for reciprocals of integers ≤ N
connection: How many rationals of height ≤ H lie in {1/x + 1/y + 1/z}? Counting 3-fold reciprocal sums is a sum-product/energy question (F33).
why: A lower bound showing the 3-fold reciprocal sumset hits a large fraction of rationals a/n with small numerator would be a density version of ES-type statements.
first_step: Compute |{1/x+1/y+1/z : x,y,z ≤ N}| ∩ {4/n} for N up to 10⁴ and the energy of the reciprocal set.

title: Sierpiński/Riesel numbers: k·2^n + 1 composite for all n via covering — a 'shifted integer always composite' phenomenon
connection: Covering congruences force k·2^n + 1 to be composite for all n. ES needs p-tied integers 4Cp + 1 to be composite WITH a divisor in a class; a covering forcing compositeness is a step in the right direction for a fixed p.
why: If for each hard p a covering-type argument forced some 4Cp + 1 (C ≤ K) to have a SMALL prime factor q ≡ −1 mod 4C·…, a witness might follow (small prime factor in the right class ⇒ witness when cofactor class matches).
first_step: For hard primes, find small primes q with q | 4Cp + 1 and q ≡ −1 (mod 4C) for some C < q (i.e. C ≡ −(4p)⁻¹ mod q with the class condition); count such (q, C) pairs with q ≤ log²p.

title: Bloom–Sisask log-barrier Roth bound and its almost-periodicity
connection: Bloom–Sisask broke the logarithmic barrier in Roth's theorem using Croot–Sisask almost periodicity; ES certificate sets are sumsets/product sets of divisor sets.
why: Croot–Sisask almost-periodicity is a general tool for showing A·B (here divisor quotients) contains long structured pieces.
first_step: Apply Croot–Sisask to the convolution 1_D * 1_{D^{-1}} on (ℤ/e)^× with D = divisor set of N and quantify the approximate periods.
refs: Bloom–Sisask, Breaking the logarithmic barrier in Roth's theorem on arithmetic progressions, arXiv:2007.03528

title: OAI 025 short Egyptian fractions O(log log b) (claimed) — length-3 specialization
connection: OAI family 025 claims every a/b is a sum of O(log log b) distinct unit fractions, sharp; ES asks for exactly 3 terms at a = 4.
why: The construction's mechanism (how denominators are chosen) could expose a 'small number of terms' greedy-plus-smooth technique; calibration of what length is cheap.
first_step: Read the OAI 025 build sources and record which step needs Θ(log log b) terms; check whether for a = 4 the construction degenerates to fewer terms.

title: Skorobogatov–Sofos: Schinzel's Hypothesis on average → ES certificate families
connection: SS prove Schinzel's Hypothesis H for 100% of polynomials in families ordered by coefficient height and deduce Hasse principle for 100% of fibred varieties; ES certificates are values of polynomials in (c,d,e) tied to p.
why: Gives a rigorous 'almost all polynomials in a family behave' statement, the polynomial analogue of 'almost all p'.
first_step: Embed the ES Type I certificate polynomial family into a family indexed by coefficients and check which statement of SS transfers (likely 'ES for 100% of a coefficient family', not ES itself).

title: Graber–Harris–Starr sections exist over ℂ(t): why identities exist geometrically but not integrally
connection: GHS: rationally connected fibrations over curves have sections; U → A¹_n has rational fibres, so sections exist over ℂ(n) and ℚ(n) (identities with rational denominators), but Mordell–Schinzel shows none integral covering square classes.
why: Makes the integrality defect precise: it's an 'integral section' problem, whose obstructions are at the special fibres (n = square).
first_step: Compute the degenerate fibres of the integral model over Spec ℤ[n] and interpret the Mordell–Schinzel barrier as nonexistence of integral sections through specific fibre components.
refs: Graber–Harris–Starr, Families of rationally connected varieties, JAMS 16 (2003)

title: Bloom/Liu–Sawhney machinery for few-term Egyptian representations with dense denominators
connection: Bloom: positive density sets contain S with Σ1/n = 1, via counting with main term + exponential sums on integers with structured anatomy. Ask what the machinery gives for k-term representations of 4/p (k fixed, small) with denominators restricted to structured sets (multiples of p with smooth cofactors).
why: Bloom's framework is the modern Fourier-analytic engine for unit-fraction existence; checking where it breaks for k = 3 localises ES's difficulty.
first_step: Read Bloom's §§2–4 and identify the minimal number of terms the method needs; check if it can handle 4/p = Σ_{i≤k} 1/n_i with k ~ 10 and n_i in a set of density zero.
alt_first_steps: [tools-0333] Track, in Bloom's argument, the minimal number of terms needed for the Fourier step and how it scales.
refs: arXiv:2112.03726 (Bloom, On a density conjecture about unit fractions)

title: Mixing of the greedy/odd-greedy Egyptian map as a Markov chain on residues
connection: The map n ↦ remainder after subtracting the greedy unit fraction acts on residues; as a Markov chain its mixing describes the distribution of remainders (cf. Tao's Syracuse analysis).
why: Mixing estimates give 'almost all' success of fixed-depth greedy-with-choice algorithms and pinpoint residue traps.
first_step: Compute the transition matrix of the remainder residue mod M for the 2-step greedy-with-choice ES search and its spectral gap.

title: ES over number fields with unit-rank ≥ 1 (unit orbits as infinite families)
connection: Over O_K with infinite unit group, U_n(O_K) may have unit-orbit families. UNIT_ORBIT_ES studied these; the native field is Diophantine equations over rings of integers (unit equations, S-unit theorems).
why: Shows what infinite symmetry does to the problem. The S-unit equation theory (Evertse–Győry) gives finiteness or infinitude results for the related unit equations.
first_step: Check whether some ES equivalent form is an S-unit equation in disguise (e.g. after fixing a factorisation pattern) and apply the S-unit counting bounds.
refs: Evertse–Győry, Unit Equations in Diophantine Number Theory (2015)
areas: ES variants, function fields & other rings

title: Restricted-denominator ES: which congruence restrictions on x, y, z keep ES true?
connection: Breusch/Stewart: every rational with odd denominator is a sum of distinct odd unit fractions (many terms). For three terms, all-odd is impossible (parity: 4xyz = p(xy+yz+zx) forces an even denominator). Classify restrictions (x,y,z in prescribed classes mod m) that are consistent with ES for all small p, and test which ones look 'every p'.
why: Restricted versions that hold numerically are stronger statements that may carry more structure for a proof (or reveal new obstructions).
first_step: Read arXiv:1108.6118 and arXiv:1606.02117; tabulate which three-term restricted variants of 4/n are known false and true.
alt_first_steps: [upgrades-0150] For m = 3, 4, 5, 8 and all class-restriction patterns, compute the failure set among p ≤ 10⁶.
refs: Breusch, A special case of Egyptian fractions, Amer. Math. Monthly 61 (1954) 200-201
areas: ES variants, function fields & other rings

title: I3 at 2^k ± 1 by exponent coverings: Sierpiński-number technique
connection: I3 holds on 2^k ± 1 etc. by exponent coverings (I3_DEEP). This is exactly the Sierpiński/Riesel-number covering technique for k·2^n + 1 compositeness.
why: Covering congruences in the exponent are a native tool that is complete for its families. Extending to 'n = a·b^k + c' families tests how far exponent coverings go.
first_step: Try families n = 3^k ± 2, 5·3^k + 1 with exponent coverings for I3; record which ones close.

title: Erdős #306-type Fourier counts (Li 2609.32140) and why abundance is needed
connection: Recent AI/Lean-assisted solutions of Erdős problems (e.g. Li's #306) use Fourier counts over exponentially many configurations. ES has polylog witnesses.
why: Calibration: these tools apply to ES variants with many more terms (k ≥ log n unit fractions). They locate the minimal k where Fourier methods work.
first_step: Find the smallest k(n) for which '4/n is a sum of k unit fractions with denominators ≤ n^C' is provable by a Fourier count; compare with k = 3.

title: Unit-fraction graph on ℚ: 3-step walks from 0 to 4/n
connection: Define the graph on ℚ_{>0} with r ~ r + 1/k. ES(n) ⇔ dist(0, 4/n) ≤ 3. Farey neighbours a/b, c/d satisfy c/d − a/b = 1/(bd), so unit steps between Farey neighbours are edges.
why: It gives a metric-geometry view of Egyptian fractions. Bounds on the graph's diameter on {m/n : m ≤ 4} are exactly ES-type statements, and 'every m/n at distance ≤ c·log log n' results are known.
first_step: Compute the distance-2 neighbourhood of 4/p (pairs 1/y + 1/z) and its overlap with {4/p − 1/x}; record which Farey structure produces most certificates.

title: Tetrahedral analogue: 1/r = Σ 1/h_i over four faces (four-term Egyptian in 3D)
connection: For a tetrahedron, 1/r = Σ_{i=1}^4 1/h_i (inradius vs altitudes). The triangle identity 1/r = Σ 1/h_i (three terms) is the 2D version behind the altitude form of ES. Higher-dimensional simplices give k-term Egyptian equations with geometric realisability conditions.
why: It places ES in a dimension ladder of simplex geometry, where realisability (simplex inequalities) adds constraints. Low priority, but it is a natural family.
first_step: Record; optionally test whether 4/n = Σ 1/h_i (4 terms) with tetrahedron realisability is always solvable.

title: Values of rational symmetric functions on ℕ³: e₂/e₃ = 4/n
connection: ES(n) ⇔ the rational symmetric function e₂/e₃ = Σ 1/x_i takes the value 4/n on ℕ³. Value sets of symmetric rational functions on integer points connect to Vieta-type substitutions and to the 'totally split cubic' item.
why: It is a symmetric-function lens. Power-sum/elementary transitions might give alternative parametrisations, e.g. through e₁ (sum) or p₂.
first_step: Write ES in (e₁, e₂, e₃) with 4e₃ = n·e₂ and study integrality of the roots via the discriminant; compute which (e₁, e₂) give totally split cubics for small n.
